# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

A monitor turns a query into a state machine that tells people when something is wrong; an SLO turns a monitor or a metric into a promise about reliability. Engineers who can read, build and triage them keep alerts useful instead of noisy.  
In this lab you work only in your browser. You read the shared monitors the instructor created, build your own seat-prefixed APM error-rate monitor that notifies nobody but you, create a monitor-based SLO, and triage an alert from its event to the failing trace and log.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can go from a triggered monitor to the failing service, trace and log line. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You will use monitor status, history and context to decide whether an alert is real. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: You can build a monitor and an SLO with sensible thresholds and no external notifications. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

Datadog alerting is a chain: a query, a threshold, a state, a message and a target. An SLO sits on top and measures reliability over time.  
*Figure: Monitor and SLO Chain — Query → Threshold → State (OK / Warn / Alert / No Data) → Notification → Triage (Service Page, Trace, Log) · SLO \= Good Events ÷ Total Events over a Window*

| Object | Built From | Answers | Key Fields |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Monitor | A metric, APM, log or composite query | Is it wrong now? | Query, thresholds, message, tags |
| Monitor status | Evaluation over a window | OK, Warn, Alert or No Data? | Status history, evaluation graph |
| SLO | A monitor or good/total events | Are we meeting our target? | Target %, time window, error budget |
| Event / triage | Alert event with context | Which trace and log explain it? | service, env, host, trace\_id |

*Figure: Alert Triage Path — Monitor Alert Event → Service Page (env:cohort) → Failed Trace → Correlated Log Line*

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Monitors, Thresholds and Notifications

A monitor evaluates a query every minute over a window (for example the last 5 minutes) and compares the result with a warning and an alert threshold. Its message and recipients are separate from the query. In a shared organisation you notify only yourself, because every notification reaches a real mailbox.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| An alert should carry service, env and a link to the right dashboard and runbook, so the first responder starts at the cause. |
|  |
| An SLO converts alerts into a promise: the remaining error budget shows whether you can still afford change. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Monitor vs SLO

A monitor answers "is it wrong right now?" and notifies people. An SLO answers "over the last 7 or 30 days, how often were we right?" and tracks an error budget. Use monitors for response and SLOs for planning and trade-offs.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake When Creating Monitors in a Shared Organisation |
| :---- |
| A learner copies the example monitor, leaves the default notification list and sends test alerts to other people's mailboxes. |
|  |
| REASON: Message recipients are easy to leave unchanged. |
|  |
| YOU MUST set recipients to your own e-mail or none, and use your seat prefix in the monitor name. |

## 3.3  Monitor Types and Their Use

| Monitor Type | Query Based On | Typical Use | This Lab |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Metric | Metric time series | Host CPU, queue length | Awareness |
| APM | Service hits, errors, latency | Error rate / p95 latency | Task 2 |
| Monitor-based SLO | One or more monitors | Reliability target | Task 3 |
| Composite | Other monitors (a && b) | Reduce noise | Lab 2 |

| 📝  How to Decide Monitor or SLO |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Do we need to wake someone now, or do we need to know whether we met our promise?" Now → monitor with thresholds and a message. Promise → SLO with a target and a window. Most services need both. |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Cannot sign in to app.datadoghq.com | Wrong site or credentials | Check the URL and your seat credentials | Use https\://app.datadoghq.com and the cohort credentials; ask the instructor |
| Shared monitors not listed | Search or tag filter too narrow | Search for "easyTravel" and clear filters | Use Manage Monitors; tell the instructor (Appendix A) |
| Monitor preview graph empty | Service, env or measure wrong | Check easytravel-backend and env:cohort | Pick the service from the list; widen the timeframe |
| SLO cannot select the monitor | Monitor type or name not found | Search for your \[u\<seat\>\] monitor | Create the monitor first; use a metric or APM monitor |
| No alert event found | Timeframe too short or the fault is off | Widen the Events timeframe to Past 2 Hours | Ask the instructor to re-run Appendix A |
| Name rejected or already used | Seat prefix missing or a classmate used the name | Compare with Section 2.3 | Use the \[u\<seat\>\] prefix exactly |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 1 MINUTE

## 7.1  Discussion Questions (pick one if time is short)

| Discussion 1 — Monitor Design |
| :---- |
| Which fields make a monitor useful for the first responder? |
| What did your message contain? |
|  |
| Key answer to explore: service, env, links, runbook and owner. |
| **Discussion 2 — Thresholds** |
| How did you choose warning and alert values? |
| What data would you use to tune them? |
|  |
| Key insight: base thresholds on real traffic and history, not on guesses. |
| **Discussion 3 — SLOs and Budgets** |
| How does an error budget change a release decision? |
| What is wrong with a 100 % target? |
|  |
| Key answer: the budget allows change; 100 % leaves no room and is rarely achievable. |
| **Discussion 4 — Triage Speed** |
| Which pivot saved the most time? |
| Which tag was essential? |
|  |
| Answer: service, env and trace\_id; consistent tags make alert-to-log a few clicks. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Notifying real people from a lab | Default recipients | Spam in a shared organisation | Own e-mail only or none |
| No seat prefix | Names look free | Collisions among 40 learners | Prefix every object with your seat |
| Alert threshold without warning | Copying examples | Late or noisy alerts | Use a warning level and review with real data |
| Editing a \[SHARED\] monitor | Looks like your own | Breaks the lab for everybody | Read only; create your own copy |
| SLO on too little data | New monitors have no history | Misleading percentage | State the window and the data volume |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (5 MINUTES BEFORE COHORT)

Instructor only. The runbook takes about 5 minutes; run it before the cohort. Learners never see or run these commands.

| ⌨  Appendix A — Instructor pre-class runbook (EC2 ip-172-30-0-220, 5 minutes before cohort) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 0: Variables (Datadog API and application keys of the KloudKraft organisation; keep them out of screenshots) |
| export DD\_API\_KEY="\<api-key\>" DD\_APP\_KEY="\<application-key\>" FAULT\_MINUTES=20 |
|  |
| \# Step 1: Verify the Agent and the Java tracer |
| sudo datadog-agent status \| grep \-E "API Key\|Hostname\|Site" \| head \-4 |
| ps \-ef \| grep \-c '\[d\]d-java-agent.jar' |
|  |
| \# Step 2: Create the two \[SHARED\] monitors if missing (no notifications; adjust metric names to your Java integration) |
| curl \-sS \-X POST "https\://api.datadoghq.com/api/v1/monitor" \-H "Content-Type: application/json" \-H "DD-API-KEY: \$DD\_API\_KEY" \-H "DD-APPLICATION-KEY: \$DD\_APP\_KEY" \\ |
|   \-d '{"name":"\[SHARED\] easyTravel Backend High p95 Latency","type":"query alert","query":"avg(last\_5m):p95:trace.servlet.request{env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend} \> 1","message":"Shared component monitor, no notifications.","tags":\["env:cohort","shared:true"\]}' |
| curl \-sS \-X POST "https\://api.datadoghq.com/api/v1/monitor" \-H "Content-Type: application/json" \-H "DD-API-KEY: \$DD\_API\_KEY" \-H "DD-APPLICATION-KEY: \$DD\_APP\_KEY" \\ |
|   \-d '{"name":"\[SHARED\] easyTravel Backend Error Rate","type":"query alert","query":"sum(last\_5m):sum:trace.servlet.request.errors{env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend}.as\_count() / sum:trace.servlet.request.hits{env:cohort,service:easytravel-backend}.as\_count() \* 100 \> 5","message":"Shared component monitor, no notifications.","tags":\["env:cohort","shared:true"\]}' |
|  |
| \# Step 3: Switch the CreditCardCheckError500 plugin on for the session, then off again |
| curl \-s "http\://localhost:8091/services/ConfigurationService/setPluginEnabled?name=CreditCardCheckError500\&enabled=true" |
| (sleep \$((FAULT\_MINUTES\*60)); curl \-s "http\://localhost:8091/services/ConfigurationService/setPluginEnabled?name=CreditCardCheckError500\&enabled=false") & |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| API Key … valid · Hostname: ip-172-30-0-220 · Site: datadoghq.com   then   a number ≥ 1 |
| Two JSON responses, each with an "id" and the monitor name |
| HTTP 200; within a few minutes the shared Error Rate monitor changes state and an alert event appears |

| :---- |
| Verify before class: all 40 learners can sign in, both \[SHARED\] monitors are visible and notification-free, learners may create monitors and SLOs, and the trial still has capacity (Browser Test cap: 5 org-wide). |
